text:
Systematic review and meta-analysis by Avni and colleagues (PLOS ONE 2015, DOI 10.1371/journal.pone.0129305) comparing vasopressors for the treatment of adult septic shock, assessing efficacy and safety across all agents.

METHODS: The authors searched MEDLINE, CENTRAL, LILACS and conference proceedings up to June 2014 and included randomized controlled trials comparing different vasopressors in adult septic shock. Thirty-two trials with 3,544 patients were included. The primary outcome was all-cause mortality; haemodynamic variables and adverse events were secondary outcomes. Risk ratios with 95% confidence intervals were pooled.

KEY FINDINGS: Compared with dopamine (866 patients, 450 events), norepinephrine (832 patients, 376 events) was associated with decreased all-cause mortality: risk ratio 0.89 (95% CI 0.81 to 0.98), corresponding to an absolute risk reduction of 11% and a number needed to treat of 9. Norepinephrine was also associated with a lower risk of major adverse events and cardiac arrhythmias than dopamine. No mortality benefit was demonstrated for norepinephrine versus epinephrine, phenylephrine, or vasopressin/terlipressin. Haemodynamic profiles were broadly similar across agents, with some advantage for norepinephrine in central venous pressure, urinary output and blood lactate levels.

CONCLUSION: The evidence supports a survival benefit, better haemodynamic profile and fewer adverse events for norepinephrine over dopamine, and the authors conclude norepinephrine should be regarded as the first-line vasopressor in septic shock. A related meta-analysis of vasopressin versus norepinephrine as first-line therapy found no mortality difference but lower odds of requiring renal replacement therapy with vasopressin (odds ratio 0.68; 95% CI 0.47 to 0.98), suggesting vasopressin as a consideration in patients at high renal risk.
title: Vasopressors for the treatment of septic shock: systematic review and meta-analysis
